# docs_audit_report — 2026-06-25

## TL;DR (stranger's 30-second take)
The hero is genuinely strong — I understand what Carnot does in one sentence and I can see `pip install carnot-ebm`. But the moment I scroll, trust erodes fast: the license contradicts itself (MIT-0 in the hero, Apache 2.0 in the footer), the "Evidence" section is a wall of insider-jargon cards with suspiciously perfect numbers (1.0, 60/60), and the blog right below it openly advertises that the project's own results were "Caught Cheating" and hit "Two Retractions." A skeptical stranger keeps the tab open for the hero but bounces at the evidence — the page undermines its own numbers.

## TOP 3 PROBLEMS
1. License self-contradiction — hero badge + `<meta>` say "MIT-0", footer says "Apache 2.0 License." A stranger checking the single most basic adoption fact gets two different answers.
2. The "Evidence" grid pairs suspiciously-perfect numbers (GSM8K TP "0.5 → 1.0", "60/60 attacks", "identical losses") with a blog section titled "Caught Cheating" / "Two Retractions" — the page itself signals its numbers may be fabricated, so why trust the rest?
3. "Evidence" is 12 dense cards drowning in undefined acronyms (EstimationVerifier, SVAMP, VeriCoT, CRANE, CCTU, PRM-BiasBench, HalluGuard v3, FoVer baseline) with decorative meter bars whose widths don't map to the claims — a stranger skims none of them.

## DETAILED FINDINGS

### Bloat
- "Evidence" results grid (#results) — 12 result cards — under the 20 cap, but each is jargon-dense and the volume guarantees zero are read. Cut to the 4-5 strongest, plainest-language wins (e.g. HumanEval code, typed constraints, the FPGA prototype).
- Hero "Recent progress" r-card (lines 309-313) — ~55 words but structurally wrong: a prose card jammed inside the headline-numbers stat bar, mixing a paragraph into what should be four glanceable numbers. It dilutes the 30-second skim. Move it out of the stat bar or cut it.
- Blog section (#writing) — 7 cards — count is fine; flagged below for credibility, not length.

- Stat bar (line 306) — "382 Completed milestones" — a stranger has no idea what a "milestone" is or why 382 of them matters; reads as internal project-management vanity.
- Hero "Recent progress" card (line 312) — "Repinned from v2 0.9857" — "repinned" and "v2 0.9857" are pure insider versioning; a stranger doesn't know what was repinned or from what.

- Preprint body (lines 593-594) — "non-operator environment", "pending operator-initiated upload" — "operator" is an internal project role; meaningless to outsiders.
- Results cards (lines 549, 559, 554, 564, 574, 569) — "EstimationVerifier SVAMP", "VeriCoT", "CRANE", "PRM-BiasBench", "CCTU", "HalluGuard v3", "k=5 ensemble", "0.125 FoVer baseline", "GSM8K" — none are defined; a conference stranger cannot decode a single one in 30 seconds.
- Test-Time Compute card (lines 497-500) — "TTC", "PREM", "Process-Reward Energy Model variance", "intrinsic motivation for continuous self-learning" — the most jargon-dense block on the page and it doesn't say what I can *check*.

### Per-milestone narrative
- Hero "Recent progress" card (line 312) — "Repinned from v2 0.9857 after pre-submission adversarial audit" — reads like a retrospective/changelog entry, not landing-page copy.
- Stat bar (line 306) — "382 Completed milestones" — internal status reporting surfaced as a headline metric.
- Preprint (lines 593-594) — "The arXiv submission is prepared but pending operator-initiated upload" — internal workflow status, not something a stranger needs.

### Inconsistencies
- License: "MIT-0" (hero badge line 291, `<meta>` line 7) vs "Apache 2.0 License" (footer line 766). Direct contradiction.
- "FoVer" used two incompatible ways: headline "0.9131 AUROC on FoVer" (line 308) vs results card "0.90 AUC (vs 0.125 FoVer baseline)" (line 550). Same name is both the flagship 0.91 result and a near-zero 0.125 baseline — irreconcilable to a stranger.
- Three competing AUROC/AUC numbers float on one page: 0.9131 (FoVer headline), 0.9857 (retracted "v2"), 0.91 (prompt-injection, line 530), 0.90 (SVAMP). A stranger can't tell which is "the" number.
- Arithmetic example mismatch: wrong answer is "47 + 28 = 76" in the intro (line 329), the success card (line 343), and the code comment (line 628) — but the "One-word-at-a-time" card (line 338) shows "47 + 28 = 7". Looks like a typo and confuses the one concrete example the page leans on.
- "Seven capabilities… What you can check" (lines 415-416) overcounts: 3 of the 7 cards (Research operations, APIs & portable memory, Test-Time Compute) are internal infrastructure, not things a user checks. The header promises checkable capabilities and delivers project internals.
- Meter bars encode nothing consistent: "+3.0 points" → 14.6% bar, "+4.9 points" → 66.7% bar, "0.91 AUROC" → 91% bar, several → 100%. The widths are decorative noise dressed as data; a stranger who notices this distrusts the whole section.

### Missing essentials
- Who maintains it: footer credits only "Ian Blenke" — no team, institution, or contributor count. A stranger reads a solo hobby project with no institutional anchor, which weakens trust for adoption.
- "Why should I trust the numbers" is actively damaged rather than merely absent: the perfect scores + self-confessed fabrication blog cut against the "every number backed by an artifact" claim.
- (Present and fine: one-sentence what-it-does, install command, GitHub/HuggingFace links.)

### Fabrication signals
- "GSM8K extraction TP rate: 0.5 → 1.0" (line 560) — a perfect 1.0 with no sample size or credibility anchor.
- "k=5 ensemble catches 60/60 attacks" (line 565) — perfect on a small (n=60) sample.
- "2.0× speedup, identical losses" (line 540) — "identical" is suspiciously clean; needs a tolerance/seed anchor.
- "0.90 AUC (vs 0.125 FoVer baseline)" (line 550) — an AUC of 0.125 is far *below* random (0.5), a bizarre baseline that itself reads as a misconfiguration or cherry-pick.
- "99.3% of wrong code flagged" (line 431) — very high on n=164; plausible but uncushioned.
- Blog card "Zero false positives" (line 741) — absolute claim with no caveat.
- Net effect: these sit directly above blog posts admitting fabricated artifacts ("Caught Cheating: 95 Microseconds on a 30B Model"), so the perfect numbers read as not-yet-caught rather than verified.

## WHAT'S WORKING
- The hero one-liner ("checks whether an answer is internally consistent — and suggests a fix when it isn't") is clear, jargon-free, and answers "what does it do" instantly. Best part of the page.
- The Problem section's `47 + 28` example and the "Extract → Check → Repair" three-step are concrete and genuinely accessible to a non-specialist (jargon leaks aside).

1. Fix the license contradiction immediately — decide MIT-0 vs Apache 2.0 and make hero, `<meta>`, and footer agree. This is a one-word credibility fix with the highest leverage.
2. Cut the "Evidence" grid from 12 cards to ~5, and rewrite each surviving card in plain English with a sample size — drop EstimationVerifier/SVAMP/VeriCoT/CRANE/CCTU/HalluGuard/PRM-BiasBench naming or gloss each in five words.
3. Resolve the "FoVer 0.9131" vs "FoVer 0.125 baseline" collision — rename one so the same word isn't both the headline and a near-zero baseline; pick ONE headline AUROC and stop showing 0.9857/0.91/0.90 alongside it without labels.
4.
